catalog_quote: Like is the case with most of the African languages south of the Sahara, Lunyole is a tonal language. The language exhibits register tone, rather than contour tone. ... The language has basically a two-tone system where each vowel may be high or low tone. Syllables with two moras, i.e. those with long vowels and pre-nasalized consonants, may on rare occasions bear a rising or falling tone. Lunyole exhibits a very light functional load with rare tonal lexical pairs and grammatical tone. ... [9.1.1] Lunyole nouns exhibit a two-tone system and four common tone patterns: HH, HL, LH, and LL. However, in some few cases a rising or falling tone may occur . These four patterns are realized on the noun with its prefix. The prefix itself may take a H, L, LH or HL tone. There is no residual floating tone in Lunyole. ... [9.4 Tone Distribution] It appears there is a free distribution of tone – both the high and low tone may occur on any syllable in a word whether on the first or last syllable. The distribution of the rising tone appears to be rare. As stated more investigation on tone has to be done with a wider range of words.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (68 pp., text layer, PDF metadata 'Lunyole Phonology Statement', created 2013; document header 'Date: 4th September, 2006, Issue 1, Status: Approved'). extracted text of p. 32 of 68, sec. 9 'TONE', reads exactly: 'Like is the case with most of the African languages south of the Sahara, Lunyole is a tonal language. The language exhibits register tone, rather than contour tone.. The language has basically a two-tone system where each vowel may be high or low tone. Syllables with two moras, i.e. those with long vowels and pre-nasalized consonants, may on rare occasions bear a rising or falling tone. Lunyole exhibits a very light functional load with rare tonal lexical pairs and grammatica…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lunyole is described purely as a two-level (H/L) register-tone language with lexical and grammatical tone contrasts of low functional load; H and L are positionally free within the word. The source (and every other opened description: Wicks 2006, Namulemu 2014, Marlo et al. 2017) makes no statement at all about word stress, accent, or a fixed prominence position.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes only: contour (rising/falling) tones are rare and confined to bimoraic syllables; vowels are automatically long before NC and after Cw/Cy (sec. 6.1.2.3); tone is not marked in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone in citation forms (nouns with augment+prefix, infinitives); Marlo et al. 2017 add phrase-level verb-tone melodies for the Lower Nyole variety. No stress domain is described anywhere.
new_statements.identity_note: Namulemu 2006, Wicks 2006 and Namulemu 2014 describe Upper Nyole / Lunyole proper (Butaleja District, mainly the Lumenya prestige dialect) = nyol1238 [nuj]. Marlo et al. 2017 describe 'Lower Nyole', a moribund resettlement variety of the same JE35 language spoken in Mayuge District, south Busoga (no separate glottocode; not to be confused with Kenyan Nyore/Olunyole JE33, nyor1246).

new_statements.quote: Lunyole is a five-vowel tonal 2 Bantu language and its general structure is similar to that of other Bantu languages of Uganda, such as Luganda and Runyoro. [...] [footnote 2:] Tone is both lexical and grammatical. There are four tones, high, mid, low and falling. Where tone is shown in this article, I have used the following conventions: high tone, / mid tone unmarked, low tone \ , falling tone > .
new_statements.citation: Morris, H. F. 1963. A note on Lunyole. Uganda Journal 27(1): 127-134.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1 Introduction, p. 127 (PDF p. 144) and footnote 2, p. 133 (PDF p. 150); sec. 2 'A Phonetic Note', pp. 127-129
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-extracted PDF pp. 143-152 of with extracted text. Article starts on PDF p. 144 (header 'Uganda Journal, 27, 1 1963, pp. 127-134 / A NOTE ON LUNYOLE / by H. F. MORRIS'); footnotes under 'NOTES' on PDF p. 150 (journal p. 133), footnote 8 onward on PDF p. 151 (p. 134). Quote 1 found verbatim, sec. 1 Introduction, p. 127: 'Lunyole is a five-vowel tonal 2 Bantu language and its general structure is similar to that of other Bantu languages of Uganda, such as Luganda and Runyoro.' Footnote 2, p. 133, verbatim: 'Tone is both lexical and grammatical. There are four tones, high, mid, low and falling. Where tone is shown in this article, I have used the following conventions: high tone, / mid tone…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog/existing statement (Namulemu 2006): tonal language, no stress or accent statement (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|promin over the article = 0 hits). Side difference in the tone analysis only: Morris posits four tones (high, mid, low, falling) where Namulemu 2006 describes a two-tone H/L register system; this bears on tone, not stress. The UFDC scan was reached through the patron API (serialhierarchy -> vid 00070 = Volume 27 (1963) Number 1 (March)) and the direct file on ufdcimages.uflib.ufl.edu; quotes checked against both the extracted text layer and UFDC's own full-text file.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lunyole is described as a tonal language with lexical and grammatical tone and four tones (high, mid, low, falling); the article says nothing about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 3 (p. 133): the description rests on the northern dialect of Bunyole county; the south-western dialect is closer to Lugwe. Sec. 2(a): five vowels each with a long and short form (vowel length is contrastive).
new_statements.identity_note: Morris 1963 (fn. 3, p. 133) is based on the northern dialect of Bunyole county (Bukedi District, Uganda), the majority variety; he notes the south-western dialect is closer to Lugwe. Schadeberg 1989 treats Nyole (Guthrie E.35 = JE35) as a Greater Luyia language and explicitly distinguishes it from Nyore (E.33) of Kenya, with which Bastin's bibliographies had confused it; his data come from Morris 1963 and Eastman 1972.
